title: Sundar's call
hookLine: Sundar records Guru Amar Das's last wishes: sing the Lord's praise, don't weep for me (Ramkali, Sadd, ang 923)

cards: Some families keep a letter in a drawer, written to be opened after a parent dies. Sometimes it holds money matters. Sometimes it says: don't make a fuss, play my favorite song, eat well.

In Raag Ramkali, on Ang 923, the Guru Granth Sahib keeps something like that letter. A poet named Sundar records what Guru Amar Das asked of his family as his life came to its end. It's called the Sadd, the call.

teach.b: In the hymn, the call is the one that comes from God at the end of a life, the summons home. Sundar, whom tradition counts in Guru Amar Das's own family, tells it as an eyewitness would.
The Guru gathers his family and speaks plainly.

teach.h: LET NO ONE WEEP FOR ME.
teach.b: In paraphrase: let no one weep for me after I'm gone; the one who weeps does not please me. Then what he wants instead: after me, sing pure kirtan.

teach.h: KIRTAN, THE LORD'S STORY, THE NAME.
teach.b: Send for the Lord's learned ones, and let them read the Lord's story. Let the Lord's Name be heard.
Then the line passes on: the Sadd tells how Guru Amar Das names Ram Das as the Guru after him, and the family bows before him.

teach.h: A DEATH, A SONG, THE LIGHT PASSED ON.
teach.b: One short hymn, three things side by side: a death, a song, and the light passing on. Look closely at what he asks. He isn't saying grief is wrong for everyone, always.
He's saying what he wants for his own going. He sees his death as being called home, so the fitting answer is praise, not wailing.
And it's recorded by someone close to him, who could have written only his own sorrow, and instead wrote down the instructions.

Tradition carries this into Sikh funerals, where kirtan and the reading of Gurbani are given the center, and the evening prayer, Kirtan Sohila, is recited. Grief comes. The Sadd gives it a song to walk alongside.

how: At Sikh funerals kirtan and the reading of Gurbani are central, and the Sadd is sometimes sung; Sikh teaching speaks of death as the soul answering God's call home.

games.q: inside the Sadd — tap the pairs.

s: the Sadd is a hymn written by Guru Amar Das himself
it's by Sundar, who records the Guru's last wishes.
in the Sadd, the Guru asks his family not to weep for him
the one who weeps, he says, does not please him.
the Sadd asks for silence after the Guru is gone
it asks for the Lord's praise, the Lord's story, and kirtan.

games.q: you're in Guru Amar Das's family as his life ends. what does he ask of you?
o: keep a long time of mourning.
sing kirtan and hear the Lord's story.
games.why: the Sadd records it plainly: don't weep for me, let there be kirtan, read the Lord's story, hear the Name.

practice: Go gently: bring to mind someone you've lost, or something that has ended, and if tears come, let them; nothing here is in a hurry.

Then find one thing about them that makes you glad, a laugh, a phrase, a song they loved, and let it come forward and fill the breath, humming a line silently if you like. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Sadd. A call, the summons home. Sundar's hymn in Raag Ramkali records Guru Amar Das's wish: when I'm gone, sing the Lord's praise, don't weep for me.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: a call; the summons home, and the name of Sundar's hymn.

carryVoice: Your line: sing, don't weep. It was the Guru's wish for his own going. That's day seven hundred ninety-four.
